what: The Heart Rate Zones Calculator works out your maximum heart rate and five training zones, from very light recovery to all-out effort.

It offers five research formulas for max heart rate (Tanaka, classic 220 − age, Gellish, Nes and Gulati) or your own measured max, and two zone methods: percentage of max, or Karvonen, which uses your resting heart rate.
uses: Know the heart rate for easy, steady and hard sessions.
Copy the numbers into a fitness watch or app.
See how different max heart rate formulas change your zones.
A falling resting heart rate shifts your Karvonen zones.
tutorial: Optional: type your resting pulse in beats per minute.
Pick a max heart rate formula, or "I know my max heart rate" and type it.
Leave "Automatic" to use Karvonen when a resting rate is entered, or choose a method.
Each zone shows its name, percentage range, bpm range and what it feels like.
Click "Copy zones" to paste them elsewhere.
features: Tanaka, 220 − age, Gellish, Nes and Gulati.
Use your own max from a test.
Zones based on heart rate reserve.

example.title: Worked example
example.text: Age 40 with the Tanaka formula: 208 − 0.7 × 40 = 180 bpm max. By % of max, zone 2 (60–70%) is 108–126 bpm. With a resting heart rate of 60, the reserve is 120, so Karvonen zone 2 is 120 × 0.6 + 60 = 132 to 120 × 0.7 + 60 = 144 bpm.

tips: Measure resting heart rate on several mornings and use the average.
Most easy training should be in zones 1–2.
Heat, caffeine, stress and poor sleep raise heart rate.
A lab or field test gives a far better max than any formula.
problems: Karvonen needs a resting heart rate
Type your resting pulse or switch to "% of max heart rate".
It must be between 25 and 120 bpm and well below your max.
Zones feel too hard or easy
Your real max may differ from the formula. Try another formula or a measured max.
